faq: What does the scale factor multiply?
Ground distances at that latitude are drawn k times larger than the same distances at the equator. To recover truth from a projected measurement, divide by k; to draw truth, multiply.
Why does the web use a distorting projection at all?

Because it is conformal (local shapes and angles are right), its tiles nest perfectly, and north is up everywhere. Navigation and street maps prize those properties over area honesty — know the trade and the map stops lying to you.
No — conformality means angles and bearings are locally true on Mercator. It is distances and areas that inflate, which is precisely the split this calculator quantifies.
k runs to infinity as latitude approaches 90°, so Web Mercator simply gives up near ±85.0511° — the standard's cutoff, and the reason polar maps use other projections.
Is EPSG:3857 really a sphere formula?
Yes — it applies spherical Mercator maths to WGS84 latitudes (hence 'pseudo-Mercator'). The calculator's sec(latitude) is the spherical local scale, the standard's own definition.
How does this connect to map tiles?
Metres per pixel at a zoom combine the equatorial pixel size with 1/k at the tile's latitude: northern tiles cover less ground per pixel, exactly by this factor.
Can I use it to fix an area I measured?
Divide the projected area by k² at the measurement's latitude for a good local correction. Large regions spanning many latitudes need true geodesic area tools instead — distortion varies across them.
